what_was_reported: An extensive coast reported in the Weddell Sea, running south from around 62 degrees south, described with landmarks and soundings.
why_plausible: Morrell was sailing in the same exceptional ice year that let Weddell reach an extraordinary latitude, in a sea that was demonstrably open that season and closed in most others. A coast reported from there in 1823 was not absurd on its face.
later_evidence: Later voyages, including the Endurance drift across much of the same water, found open sea and pack where the coast was placed.
notes: The programme's strongest ghost case after Wilkes, and the one that connects Act VI directly to Act VIII: Endurance drifted through the water Morrell had charted as land. Morrell's reliability is separately disputed in the literature, which is a question about the man and not about the feature, and the two are kept apart. No cause is attributed.

what_was_reported: A range reported to the south of the Ross Sea coast and named after Ross's former commander.
why_plausible: Ross was an experienced observer working in clear polar air, where distance and elevation are notoriously hard to judge and where a far snowfield can read as a nearer range.
later_evidence: Later parties working over the same ground did not find a range as charted.
notes: Included because the claimant is the most reliable observer in the dataset. A ghost feature attributable to a careless witness teaches nothing; one attributable to Ross is the whole argument of Act VI. The plausibility note stops short of naming refraction as the cause, because no source is held for that.

what_was_reported: An island reported in the far South Pacific, with a described position, subsequently repeated on charts and searched for by later vessels.
why_plausible: A single reported position in an ocean nobody crossed often, in an era when a chart had no way to record that a feature rested on one unconfirmed report.
later_evidence: Reported to have been searched for without result and eventually removed from charts. No authority for the removal is held here.
notes: A sub-Antarctic phantom rather than a continental one, kept because it is the clearest case of the pattern the reusable methodology is for: report, repetition, search, removal. Filed as unresolved rather than disproved: the removal is reported but no authority for it is held, and the validator refuses a disproof that cannot name what disproved it. Ramsay is a popular survey and the audit has already ruled that it may not carry an individual case.

claimant: Anonymous; the history printed at Paris by Claudio Barbin in 1677
what_was_reported: A peopled part of the Terra Australe lying opposite Persia. Persian pilots bound for the East Indies were carried there by winds and sea storms and forced to land; word of the discovery reached Sevaris, high priest of the Sun, who went with armed ships to take possession, was made master of the country, and built a city he named Sevarinde with a temple to the Sun. The two peoples he found, the Prestarambi and the Strucarambi, were called Sevarambi after him. Coronelli takes the account from a history printed at Paris by Claudio Barbin in 1677.
why_plausible: A southern continent opposite Persia was ordinary geography in 1677, and the report arrived in the shape a true discovery took: a storm-driven landfall, a return to a known port, and a printed relation. Coronelli himself calls the things told of them close to dreamed and touching on the incredible, which is a judgement about the contents and not about the form.
later_evidence: Coronelli rules the history suspect in 1691 and gives his grounds: no author's name is attached; the circumstances described are paradoxical; and the same history dates the discovery to 1427, so two and a half centuries would have passed without a word of it reaching European countries. He adds an anachronism, that a great priest of the Sun could not have ruled in Persia in that century, Persia having been under Islamic law since Mohammed's lifetime.
source_locator: Atlante Veneto Tomo I, 'Terre Polari, Artiche, ed Antartiche', printed page 76 (Rumsey 12186.107)
notes: The first of the two invented countries Coronelli recounts at length before rejecting them, and the fullest rejection on the page: he argues from the missing author, the internal implausibility, the silence of two and a half centuries and a dated anachronism. claimant: Not named by Coronelli; a narrative attributed to the descendants of Giorgio Pines and printed at Roano in 1668
what_was_reported: An island to the south of Africa. In Coronelli's telling some Englishmen sent four vessels in 1589, in the reign of Queen Elizabeth, to establish the East India trade; one was wrecked on the unknown coasts of the south and none survived but a young man named Giorgio Pines and four women, one of them a Moor. A Flemish ship thrown to the island by bad weather in 1667 found the five multiplied to ten or twelve thousand, speaking English, holding a written descent left by Pines at his death aged eighty; a descendant gave it to the Fleming to keep the memory, and it was printed at Roano in 1668.

claimant: Lozieres and Courtais, French captains of Saint Malo
what_was_reported: A country said to have been discovered in 1650 by two French captains of Saint Malo, Lozieres and Courtais, who placed it on the confines of Lapland and of the Samoyeds and divided it into twelve provinces: Frisquemorenna, Sainctyonide, Taupierie, Tillitie, Brossieride, Pichotelanne, Clauzellique, Gadrettona, Sovillacia, Godefrira, Touronnide and Fresnence. The relation was printed at Paris in 1662.

what_was_reported: A coast of the Terra Australe described on some geographical charts to the south of the Cape of Good Hope, from which a cape runs out at 42 degrees of southern latitude. claimant: Not named by Coronelli; the landfall is reported of the Frenchman Gonneville
what_was_reported: A land placed on the charts next to the Terra di Vista, south of the Cape of Good Hope. Some report, Coronelli writes, that a Frenchman called Gonneville arrived there in 1504 and was received by a petty king named Arosca, and that after several months he took home to Normandy some people of that country, among them Essomerice Meriu, the son of one of those kings.
why_plausible: Alone in this list the story has a named traveller, a named host and named people carried back to Normandy, where they could in principle have been met. That is the strongest form a report of an unvisited land can take, and it is the form a chart has no way to distinguish from a true one.
later_evidence: As with the Terra di Vista, Coronelli gives no verdict in the sentence itself. The next paragraph opens 'Queste Favole si possono aggiungere' and takes both names into the fables with the City of Tartar, Manoa del Dorado and the rest.

claimant: Not named by Coronelli, who gives the name without its author
what_was_reported: A strait, named without position, description or discoverer in a list of chart features Coronelli says are believed to be fictitious.
why_plausible: A supposed discovery lay behind it, which is the premise of Coronelli's own reason for rejecting it, and the charts had carried it long enough for him to have to name it. Nothing further can be said from this page.
later_evidence: Coronelli lists it in 1691 among the features 'Vengono pure creduti Fititij', held to be fictitious, and gives a single reason for the whole group rather than one for each: after their supposed discoveries nobody was ever again able to find them or to see them.
source_locator: Atlante Veneto Tomo I, 'Terre Polari, Artiche, ed Antartiche', printed page 76 (Rumsey 12186.107)
notes: A north-western American strait, not a southern feature.
